analysis.one_liner: Reopens FHA mortgage insurance to seller-financed downpayments, with credit-score tiers, counseling, and appraisal protections.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee reported the bill with an amendment on October 2, 2008, but it never received a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended; its 28 cosponsors split 20 Democrats and 8 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: Just months after Congress barred FHA buyers from using downpayment 'gifts' funded by the home seller, this bill would carve exceptions back in. Borrowers with stronger credit could use seller-financed downpayments, with premium caps for mid-range scores and a no-taxpayer-subsidy condition for the weakest scores. The committee version also blocks HUD's planned credit-score-based premium scheme except for a flexible structure for borrowers scoring under 600, requires downpayment-assistance programs to offer counseling, and lets HUD fine people who pressure appraisers.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers without savings for a downpayment could buy FHA-insured homes using downpayments furnished by the seller or a program the seller reimburses, as long as their credit qualified. The nonprofit and government programs that channel these seller-funded gifts would regain their business, and home sellers and builders could again sell to buyers who bring no cash.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates exceptions to the existing FHA prohibition on seller-financed downpayments, making such mortgages insurable for borrowers at three credit tiers: 680 or above, 620 to 679 with capped premiums, and 619 or below starting in fiscal 2010 only if the Secretary certifies the loans need no taxpayer credit-subsidy appropriation [S2][S3][S4].

Any entity providing the downpayment assistance must offer the buyer homeownership counseling before closing, and private nonprofits in these programs must adopt conflict-of-interest policies barring their directors, officers, employees, and families from profiting from vendors to the program [S3][S4].
HUD may impose civil money penalties on anyone who compensates, coerces, or pressures an appraiser to inflate the value of a property being bought with a seller-financed downpayment [S3][S4].

The committee version blocks HUD from carrying out its planned broad risk-based premium scheme keyed to borrowers' credit scores, allowing a flexible premium structure only for borrowers with FICO scores under 600, with 30 days' notice to Congress, annual reports, and refunds of premium overcharges for borrowers who pay on time [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Homebuyers, who can end up paying for the 'gift' through a higher purchase price and with interest over the life of the mortgage, plus higher insurance premiums in the lower credit tiers. The FHA insurance fund, which taxpayers ultimately stand behind, bears any losses if these loans default at higher rates; the bill tries to hold the fund harmless by requiring premiums high enough to avoid a credit-subsidy appropriation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Buyers and the FHA insurance fund

drawbacks.text: The downpayment money comes from the seller or a party benefiting from the sale, and a seller can recover it by charging a higher price, so the 'gift' is largely built into the loan and repaid by the buyer with interest [S4].

Congress had just prohibited these arrangements in the FHA Modernization Act of 2008 (Public Law 110-289) — this bill strikes that prohibition's operative language — because seller-funded downpayment loans had been straining the FHA fund; the bill would partially reverse that judgment [S4].
Borrowers in the middle and lower credit tiers would pay higher single and annual premiums, and borrowers under 600 could face a variable premium structure set to their credit risk [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a genuine path to homeownership for buyers who have income and decent credit but no savings, and the committee added real guardrails: credit tiers, premium caps, counseling, appraisal penalties, and a requirement that the loans need no taxpayer subsidy. But the core mechanism is leaky: a seller-funded 'gift' tends to reappear as a higher price, so buyers finance their own downpayment at mortgage rates, and if these loans default at the elevated rates that led Congress to bar them months earlier, the FHA fund — and ultimately taxpayers — absorb the difference.

outcome.mechanism: The Financial Services Committee approved it and it sat on the House calendar, but no floor vote was ever scheduled before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Green (D-TX) introduced the bill on July 31, 2008, with original cosponsors including Rep. Gary Miller (R-CA), Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), and Rep. Christopher Shays (R-CT) [S4].
The House Financial Services Committee marked the bill up on September 16, 2008, ordered it reported amended by voice vote, and reported it to the House on October 2, 2008 as H. Rept. 110-905 [S6].

The committee rewrote the bill's approach to premiums: the introduced version authorized HUD's planned risk-based premium product, while the reported version prohibited that scheme and allowed flexible premiums only for borrowers with FICO scores under 600 [S2][S3][S4].
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar (No. 582) on October 2, 2008, but the House never voted on it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4][S6].
The prohibition on seller-financed downpayments that the bill sought to reverse took effect, ending the seller-funded downpayment channel for FHA loans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The FHA insurance fund and the taxpayers behind it were spared a class of loans prone to elevated default, and the seller-funded downpayment ban stayed in force; buyers without savings for a downpayment lost one route to buying a home.

for.what_they_did: His committee marked up the bill, ordered it reported by voice vote, and reported it to the House with an amendment on October 2, 2008.

against.name: Housing officials under President George W. Bush

against.what_they_did: Publicly argued that seller-financed downpayment loans defaulted at far higher rates and drained the FHA insurance fund, and supported the ban enacted earlier in 2008 that this bill would have loosened.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at every recorded stage: 28 cosponsors split 20 Democrats and 8 Republicans, the original cosponsors included two Republicans, and the committee reported the bill by voice vote; the bill's failure was a scheduling decision, not a recorded party vote.

industries.note: The bill restores and locks in the seller-funded downpayment channel that these fee-charging nonprofits and programs operate, making them the standing conduit for FHA downpayment 'gifts' while adding counseling and conflict-of-interest rules. The fees are paid by sellers and recovered through the sale, so the cost lands in buyers' loan balances.

Seller-funded downpayments let sellers close sales with buyers who bring no cash of their own. Part of the higher purchase price recaptures the 'gift,' so the seller's gain comes partly out of the buyer's mortgage balance.
More borrowers become eligible for FHA-insured loans, giving lenders more originatable mortgages with the default risk borne by the FHA insurance fund.

The committee version bars HUD from carrying out its planned broad risk-based premium scheme based on credit scores, except for a flexible structure for borrowers under 600 — protecting mid-range-credit borrowers from score-based premium hikes.
